tour.title: Old Town & the Harbour: A Lakeside City on Foot
tour.summary: A flat loop through the old town and the reclaimed harbour: a 1920s railway palace, the tower that once topped the world, a locomotive shed, an urban beach built on landfill, a market older than the city, and a whisky works turned arts district.
tour.overviewText:
Stand at the foot of Bay Street and you can see the whole argument of this city in one sweep: a 1920s railway palace, a 1970s concrete spike, a wall of glass towers, and beyond them a lake that people have spent two centuries pushing south.

Toronto is the capital of Ontario and, with about 2.8 million people, the largest city in Canada and the fourth-largest in North America. Its name comes from a Mohawk word, tkaronto — usually translated as "where there are trees standing in the water" — which described a narrows far to the north; the British borrowed it for a fort and then for the town they laid out here in 1793, which they called York, as the capital of Upper Canada, the colony that became Ontario. It was a British colonial port on Lake Ontario, and what made it matter was position: a harbour on the Great Lakes, joined by the St. Lawrence River to the Atlantic, and from the 1850s the meeting point of the country's railways. Grain, timber and manufactured goods moved through here, and the fortunes they made built the streets you are about to walk.

Then the country changed, and the city changed with it. Canada adopted official multiculturalism in 1971, and immigration remade Toronto: about half of its residents were born outside Canada, more than 200 ethnic origins are recorded among them, and the city's Christians, Muslims, Hindus, Sikhs, Jews and Buddhists share the same downtown blocks. The money is still here — finance, government, film, technology, and a waterfront that is now mostly condos instead of warehouses — but the fight now is about who can afford to live in it. Toronto's housing is among the least affordable in the world; supporters of the building boom call it supply, critics call it speculation, and both are standing in the skyline you can see from here.

The walk is shaped like a loop through the old town and the harbour. You start at Union Station, head west to the tower and the water, then turn east along the quays to the market and finish in the Distillery District. It is about 5 kilometres and roughly seventy minutes of walking before you count the time you spend inside places — flat, paved and step-free almost everywhere. The one long stretch is Queens Quay; if the heat gets to you in late August, the 509 Harbourfront streetcar runs the whole way and costs C$3.30 a ride with a tap card.

Practically: the market and the Distillery are free to enter, the CN Tower is about C$47 for an adult and the railway museum about C$18, and hours and prices move — verify at the gate. Late August is hot and humid, so carry water and start in the morning to beat the crowds, or leave it until mid-afternoon and catch the tower turning gold at sunset.

Toronto is not a city that shouts. Give it a day on foot and it will explain itself.
tour.difficulty: Easy. The whole route is flat and paved, with step-free access at every stop; the only long leg is the walk east along Queens Quay, about 2.3 kilometres, which the 509 streetcar can cover. Expect crowded aisles in the market on Saturdays and long queues at the CN Tower in August.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 9:30 to 10am so you reach the CN Tower before the worst queues and the market by lunch. Late August is hot and humid, so carry water; alternatively start mid-afternoon and time the tower for the last hour before sunset, when the lake and the skyline both turn gold.

stops.name: Union Station
stops.narration:
Start under the colonnade, because this building is the reason the city grew the way it did. Union Station opened in 1927, and its name is literal: it was the joint project of two rival railways, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific, who pooled their tracks into one "union" station rather than build two. The architecture is Beaux-Arts — the grand, symmetrical, classical style that North American cities used for banks, museums and stations in the early 1900s — designed by the Montreal firm Ross and Macdonald. Walk in through the Front Street doors and stop in the Great Hall: 76 metres long, 27 metres high at the vault, the ceiling made of interlocking Guastavino tiles (thin clay tiles set in mortar, a Catalan technique that builds a vault without a heavy stone roof), the floor of Tennessee marble, and the names of Canadian destinations carved under the cornice.

Now look at how busy it is. Union handles more than 70 million passengers a year — more than half of all Canadian inter-city rail travellers and about nine in ten of the region's commuter-rail passengers. That is why this is a good place to meet Toronto. It is the arrival hall of a country that filled up by train.

Which brings you to the tunnels. Under your feet is the PATH, 30 kilometres of underground walkways connecting more than 70 buildings and five subway stations, with 371,600 square metres of shops — Guinness World Records calls it the largest underground shopping complex in the world. It began in 1900 as a single tunnel under James Street so Eaton's shoppers could cross without their hats blowing off, and it grew because of climate: Toronto winters bring snow, ice and wind-chill, and summers are humid enough that a covered route is a gift in July and August too. The city planner Matthew Lawson pushed the idea in the 1960s. Critics then and now — Jane Jacobs among them — argued that cities die when street life moves indoors. Both things are true: the PATH is convenient, and it drains the sidewalks.

Step back outside and look east along Front Street. The low, dark stone building is a former Bank of Montreal branch from 1885; inside it is the Hockey Hall of Fame, where the Stanley Cup sits in a bank vault. Hockey is not just a sport here; it is the city's self-image, and the fact every Torontonian knows is that the Maple Leafs have not won the Cup since 1967 — the longest drought in the league. Then turn south. The tower you can see over the station is where we are going.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk through the station and the PATH. Trains, the Hockey Hall of Fame and other attractions inside are ticketed separately.
stops.openingHours: The station is open to the public roughly 5am to 1am daily. The PATH is officially open 24/7, though many access points lock at night and on weekends. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Fully accessible: level entrances, lifts to the concourses and the PATH, and step-free platforms. The Great Hall floor is smooth marble.
stops.insiderTip: In the Great Hall, look up at the carved names under the cornice — the destinations the two founding railways served in 1927. And find the oldest tunnel in the PATH, the 1900 Eaton's passage.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the Front Street doors, turn right and walk west along Front Street West for about 700 metres to the base of the CN Tower. If it is raining, take the enclosed SkyWalk from the station's western concourse instead — it connects Union to the tower and Rogers Centre without going outside.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Matt MacGillivray, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: CN Tower
stops.narration:
Look up. The CN Tower is 553.3 metres tall, and when it was completed in 1976 it was the tallest free-standing structure on Earth — a title it held until 2007, when the Burj Khalifa in Dubai overtook it. It is still the tallest free-standing structure in the Western Hemisphere. The "CN" is Canadian National, the Crown-owned railway that built it, and the reason was not tourism: Toronto's new downtown skyscrapers were blocking television and microwave signals, and broadcasters needed an antenna at least 300 metres up. A tower that tall also happened to be a monument, and CN knew it.

The engineering is worth a moment. The concrete core was poured in a slipform — a steel platform that jacked itself up about six metres a day while the concrete below set — and the whole 553-metre shaft is true to vertical within 29 millimetres. The antenna was flown up in 36 pieces by a Sikorsky Skycrane helicopter nicknamed Olga, which saved months of work. The original plan was for a bigger development called Metro Centre around it; that was cancelled, which is why for years the tower stood alone in a sea of railway land and parking lots. What you see around it now — condos, the stadium, Ripley's Aquarium — is the filling-in of that hole.

Two more things. Under the main pod there is a glass floor at 342 metres, installed in 1994 and strong enough to take 4.1 megapascals of pressure, which is engineer for "yes, it will hold you". And at 356 metres there is the EdgeWalk, opened in 2011, where you are tethered to a rail and walk around the outside of the pod — the world's highest hands-free walk of its kind, closed in winter and during storms. The 360 Restaurant up top completes one rotation every 72 minutes.

Beside you is Rogers Centre, opened in 1989 as SkyDome: the first stadium in the world with a fully retractable motorised roof, home of the Toronto Blue Jays, with a 348-room hotel built into it — 70 of those rooms look straight down onto the field. To build it, the city demolished the CN Spadina Roundhouse, one of the two great locomotive sheds that used to stand here. You will see what replaced the other one in a few minutes.

Practically: general admission to the Main Observation Level is C$47 for an adult, and The Top — 33 storeys higher, the highest observation platform in the Western Hemisphere — adds about C$12; taxes are extra, and prices move, so check at the gate or online. It is open daily, typically from mid-morning until around 10pm in summer, with timed entry and a last admission before close; book ahead in August. The tower is fully accessible, with glass-fronted lifts. If you would rather not pay, the plaza at the base and the view of the tower from Roundhouse Park are free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Adult general admission to the Main Observation Level is C$47; The Top adds about C$12 and taxes are extra. Prices and hours change — verify at the gate or on the tower's website.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, typically from mid-morning until around 10pm in summer, with timed entry and a last admission before close. Hours shorten in winter. Book ahead in August.
stops.accessibility: Fully accessible: level entrance, glass-fronted lifts and step-free observation levels. EdgeWalk is not accessible and is closed in winter and during storms.
stops.insiderTip: Buy the cheaper Main Observation Level ticket and add The Top once you are up there — it costs the same and keeps your plans flexible. The glass floor and the open-air terrace are on the lower observation level.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come down and walk west across the plaza to Bremner Boulevard, then follow the signs into Roundhouse Park — the brick semicircle with the turntable in front of it, about 300 metres away.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Scott Webb scottwebb, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Roundhouse Park & Steam Whistle
stops.narration:
You are standing in a locomotive workshop. This is the John Street Roundhouse, built for the Canadian Pacific Railway between 1929 and 1931 to replace an 1897 shed on the same spot. A roundhouse is exactly what it sounds like: a semicircular building of stalls arranged around a turntable, so a locomotive can be turned and driven into its own bay for servicing. This one had 32 stalls and a 120-foot turntable, the largest on the CPR system. Engines maintained here ran so well that crews across the network could tell a "John Street polish" by ear and eye. Then diesel arrived, steam vanished, and the roundhouse was last used for its original job in 1986.

Look at the shape today and you can read the city's priorities. One third of the building was dismantled so the Metro Toronto Convention Centre could be built underneath it, then rebuilt in 1995; that third is now Steam Whistle Brewing, which has made exactly one beer — a Czech-style pilsner — since 2001, on the principle "do one thing really, really well". The other two-thirds hold the Toronto Railway Museum, opened in 2010, and an entertainment complex. The park is a national historic site, designated in 1990, and it is free to wander.

The outdoor collection is the good part for a walker: five full-size locomotives including Canadian National 6213, a 1942 4-8-4, and Canadian Pacific 7020, a 1944 diesel switcher; passenger cars, a boxcar, a vinegar tank car and a crane; the coaling tower and water tank from the steam years; and Don Station, an 1896 wooden railway station moved here from the east end and now the ticket office. The turntable still turns. In summer a miniature railway runs a loop of the park.

Here is the fact that reframes the whole district. Everything you have walked across today — Union Station's tracks, the tower, the stadium, this park — sits on what were the Railway Lands, the vast switching yards that made Toronto the transshipment hub of Canada: grain from the prairies, timber, and manufactured goods all moved through here by rail and lake freighter. When the yards moved north in the 1960s, the land became the biggest redevelopment opportunity in the city, and this walk is basically crossing it.

Practically: the park is free and open all day. The Toronto Railway Museum charges about C$18 for an adult (HST included) — summer hours roughly noon to 5:30pm daily from mid-May to early September, winter hours Wednesday to Sunday noon to 5pm, closed Monday and Tuesday — and the mini train about C$10 in season. Steam Whistle's brewery tours are ticketed and book up; check both before you count on them. The museum's tour route has steps and is not step-free; the park itself is flat.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The park is free and open all day. The Toronto Railway Museum is about C$18 for an adult (HST included) and the mini train about C$10 in season; Steam Whistle's brewery tours are ticketed. Verify hours and prices at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Park open all day. Toronto Railway Museum: roughly noon to 5:30pm daily from mid-May to early September; in winter, Wednesday to Sunday noon to 5pm, closed Monday and Tuesday. Steam Whistle and the museum keep their own hours — check before relying on them.
stops.accessibility: The park is flat and step-free. The railway museum's tour route has steps and is not fully accessible, and Steam Whistle says its historic production-floor tour is not wheelchair accessible.
stops.insiderTip: Find Canadian National 6213, the 1942 4-8-4 steam locomotive, and read its number plate. Then look for the "John Street polish" story on the museum signs — this shed's crews were famous for it.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south out of the park, cross Lake Shore Boulevard at the lights and follow the path down to Queens Quay West. Turn right (west) and follow the waterfront about 700 metres, past the wave deck, to the sand and yellow umbrellas of HTO Park.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Arild Vågen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Harbourfront & HTO Park
stops.narration:
Stand on the sand and look at the water, then look down. That sand, and the concrete under it, is fill. The shoreline you are standing on did not exist when this city was founded — in 1793 the water's edge was up near today's Front Street, roughly half a kilometre behind you. Toronto has spent two centuries pushing the lake south.

Here is how. In the 1840s the city proposed a 30-metre-wide road called the Esplanade just south of Front Street, and made new "water lots" by cribbing and filling the shallows. The railways paid for much of the infill in exchange for a rail easement, and the Esplanade project was finished by 1865. A second, bigger fill around 1910 created Queen's Quay and the ground you are on now — these quays were concrete infill finished by 1929. A third fill in the 1950s extended the shore east of Yonge Street to make room for the Redpath Sugar Refinery, which is still working, and the marine terminals. The old harbour has shrunk from about 870 hectares in 1834 to about 490 today, and that is why the map looks like a city that grew a second, straighter waterfront.

HTO Park itself opened in 2007 on those quays. The name is a joke: HTO is a play on H2O — two hydrogens and an oxygen — with "TO", the local shorthand for Toronto, standing in for the second hydrogen, so the formula reads as a beach. The yellow umbrellas are a deliberate nod to Georges Seurat's painting "A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte". The chairs are Muskoka chairs — the Canadian version of the Adirondack chair, named for the cottage country north of here.

Out in the water are the Toronto Islands — 15 small islands, the largest urban car-free community in North America, with a school, a church and about 300 homes whose sale is tightly controlled by provincial law. They began as a sand spit: currents carry sand eroded from the Scarborough Bluffs, 10 kilometres east, westward along the lake, and that built a peninsula which storms cut loose in 1852 and again permanently in 1858. Ferries run from the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal at the foot of Bay Street; Billy Bishop airport sits on the western tip.

Two more things worth knowing. This land was, and is, Mississauga of the Credit territory — the Toronto Purchase, or Treaty 13, was renegotiated in 1805, and in 2010 the federal government paid the Mississaugas C$145 million to settle claims that the original deal was invalid and the compensation inadequate. And the concrete highway behind you is the Gardiner Expressway, which cut the waterfront off from downtown for decades; the city is still arguing about whether to tear parts of it down. The beach, the trail and the ferry docks are all free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The beach, the Martin Goodman Trail and the ferry docks are all open to the public; only boat rides and cafés charge.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours; the park is busiest on summer afternoons and evenings. Harbourfront Centre's free summer concerts and its winter ice rink run on their own seasonal schedules.
stops.accessibility: Flat, paved and step-free along Queens Quay and the Martin Goodman Trail, with benches throughout. The sand is firm but is not a paved surface.
stops.insiderTip: Walk ten minutes west along the Martin Goodman Trail to the Canada Malting silos and Ireland Park, the famine memorial — the last industrial remnants of the working harbour, with the skyline behind them.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue east along Queens Quay West for about 2.3 kilometres, keeping the water on your right; the route is flat and mostly traffic-free. If the heat is winning, tap onto the 509 Harbourfront streetcar at any stop on Queens Quay and ride to Union, then take the 504 King streetcar east to Jarvis — the market is a short walk north.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Fabian Roudra Baroi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: St. Lawrence Market
stops.narration:
You are in Old Town, the original ten blocks of the town of York. When the British laid out this settlement in 1793 — chosen as the capital of Upper Canada, the colony that became Ontario — the grid ran from George Street to Berkeley Street, Adelaide to Front. This market has been here, in one form or another, since 1803, when Lieutenant-Governor Peter Hunter's proclamation set aside a weekly market day and a patch of ground because farmers and merchants had nowhere to sell. It is older than the city itself: York was renamed and incorporated as Toronto in 1834.

Read the buildings. The South Market, where the food halls are, goes back to 1845 — it was built as Toronto's City Hall and served as the seat of municipal government until 1899, when the city moved to the grand Romanesque building at Queen and Bay. Part of that old city hall was folded into the market building you see, rebuilt in 1904. Across Front Street, the new North Market building opened in 2025, on foundations that archaeologists found belonged to the 1831, 1851 and 1904 market buildings; it holds the courthouse and, on Saturdays, the farmers' market that has run here since the 19th century.

Inside, walk the aisles slowly. The signature thing to eat is a peameal bacon sandwich: peameal bacon is back bacon — the lean eye of the pork loin — cured but not smoked, rolled in cornmeal and griddled. It is called peameal because the original coating was ground yellow peas, and it is Toronto's own sandwich; several counters sell them and the queues tell you which. Also look for the Market Gallery, upstairs in the old council chamber, which mounts exhibitions from the city's archives.

The context to carry out with you: for most of the 19th century this square was the centre of civic life, where auctions were held and public punishments carried out, and where the town's bylaws once required that butter, eggs, meat and vegetables be sold only here on market day. The Great Fire of 1849 burned the north side of the market block; St. Lawrence Hall, the 1850 concert and assembly hall across the street, was part of the rebuild. The market was named the world's best food market by National Geographic in 2012, which is a nice thing to know and a reason to come early.

Practically: entry is free. The South Market's food halls are open Tuesday to Friday roughly 9am to 7pm, Saturday 7am to 5pm and Sunday 10am to 5pm, closed Monday; the Saturday farmers' market in the North Market runs about 5am to 3pm. Holiday hours differ and stalls keep their own hours, so verify at the gate or on the market's website before you plan a meal around it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; you pay only for what you eat or buy. Stalls and the Market Gallery keep their own hours.
stops.openingHours: South Market food halls: Tuesday to Friday roughly 9am to 7pm, Saturday 7am to 5pm, Sunday 10am to 5pm, closed Monday. Saturday farmers' market in the North Market roughly 5am to 3pm. Holiday hours differ — verify on the day.
stops.accessibility: Level entrances and wide aisles on the main floor; the Market Gallery upstairs is reached by stairs or a lift. Some aisles are narrow and very busy on Saturdays.
stops.insiderTip: Come on a Saturday morning if you can — the farmers' market is the reason the market exists. If you cannot, aim for a weekday lunch and try a peameal bacon sandwich from one of the counters.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the Front Street doors, turn left and walk east along Front Street East about 1.1 kilometres to Parliament Street, then turn right and walk south one block to Mill Street and the Distillery District gate. The 504 King streetcar eastbound from King and Jarvis is a short alternative if you are tired.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Canmenwalker, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Distillery District
stops.narration:
Walk in through the gate off Trinity Street and you are inside a factory that ran for more than 150 years. Gooderham & Worts began in 1832 as a milling business — James Worts, a miller from Diss in England, built a windmill here on the waterfront near the mouth of the Don River, and his brother-in-law William Gooderham joined him. Within a few years there was more grain than the mill could sell, so in 1837 they started distilling it, and the whisky made them rich. By the 1860s this complex produced about a quarter of all the spirits made in Canada; by the 1870s, under William's son George Gooderham, output passed two million gallons a year, roughly half the country's total, and the company was one of Toronto's largest employers.

The windmill and the wharf are gone, but more than 40 buildings from the 1850s to the 1920s survive — the Stone Distillery, malt house, cooperage, kilns, tank houses, rack houses — the largest collection of Victorian-era industrial architecture in North America. That is why it was made a National Historic Site in 1988, and why the distillery kept running here until 1990, long after the neighbourhood around it had emptied out. For a decade the empty buildings were mostly a film set — "Chicago", "X-Men" and "Tommy Boy" all shot here — before a developer bought the site and reopened it in May 2003 as a pedestrian district, with a rule that no chains or franchises could lease space. That rule is why the shops are small and odd, and it is the single best thing about the place.

Two stories from the industry years. In 1916 Ontario passed the Temperance Act, banning the retail sale of alcohol in the province; the company survived by exporting to Quebec and beyond, and by making antifreeze, which the war effort and the new automobile industry both needed. And when the United States went dry in 1920, Canadian distillers had a decade of legal, lucrative business selling to middlemen who smuggled it south — in 1928 Gooderham & Worts itself was convicted of tax evasion and fined C$439,744 after the bootlegger Rocco Perri testified that he had bought its whisky. Prohibition made this district rich twice.

Look around the edges and you see the argument about modern Toronto. The Distillery is ringed by new towers; the athletes' village for the 2015 Pan American Games, just east, became housing, some of it affordable. The city's housing is among the least affordable in the English-speaking world — prices more than doubled between 2011 and 2022 before easing — and every new building here is, depending on who you ask, either the solution or the problem. Supporters point to supply and the tax base; critics to speculation and the loss of what was there before.

That is the end of the walk. You have crossed a railway empire, a broadcast tower, a filled-in lake, a market older than the city, and a whisky works turned art district — which is, more or less, the story of Toronto in five kilometres. The Distillery is free to enter and open daily, with shops generally around 10am or 11am to 6pm or 7pm and restaurants later; hours vary by business and season, so check at the gate.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the district; shops, restaurants, tours and the winter market are priced separately.
stops.openingHours: The district is open daily and free to walk. Shops generally open around 10am or 11am and close around 6pm or 7pm; restaurants and bars run later. Hours vary by business and season — check on the day.
stops.accessibility: The lanes are brick-paved, mostly level and pedestrian-only, with some uneven patches and a few door thresholds. It is one of the most walkable stretches of the route.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the chimney stack over the Boiler House and the big yellow "still" sculptures in the lanes; then walk to Trinity Street, the district's widest lane, which works as its public square.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. To get back, the 504 King streetcar on King Street East, a few minutes' walk north, runs west to Union and the subway, and taxis or rideshares pick up from Trinity Street. If you have time left, the St. Lawrence Market and Union Station are both on the way back — or stay for dinner, which is what the district is for.
